title: Statistics in psychology
examples: When should I use descriptive statistics versus inferential statistics?
What is the difference between a p-value and a significance level?
How do I know which statistical test to use for my data?

explain.say: Today we explore statistics in psychology. We learn to describe data and test ideas. First we look at descriptive statistics. This helps summarize what we observe in our data.
The mean is the average of all your numbers. You add them up and then divide by the count. For example, if scores are two and four, the mean is three.
The median is the exact middle value when data is ordered. If you have three numbers, the median is the one in the middle position. For example, in five, ten, fifteen, the median is ten.
Next we cover inferential statistics. This lets us make educated guesses about a larger group. We use small samples to draw conclusions about populations. This is key for research.
We test for statistical significance using hypotheses. We test if an observed effect is real or just due to chance. A low p-value suggests the result is unlikely to be random.
Choosing the right test depends on your data type and design. For comparing two groups, a t-test might be appropriate. For relationships, correlation is useful. You must check assumptions first.

faq.a: The p-value tells you the probability of seeing your results if there was actually no real effect. A small p-value suggests your result is probably not due to random chance.
asks: How do I interpret the p-value?

faq.q: When do I use descriptive versus inferential statistics?
faq.a: Use descriptive when you just want to summarize the data you collected. Use inferential when you want to generalize those findings to a larger population.
asks: Can I use both types of statistics?
What is the difference between describing and predicting?

faq.q: How do I decide between a t-test and an ANOVA?
faq.a: A t-test compares means between exactly two groups. ANOVA compares means between two or more groups simultaneously.
asks: When is ANOVA better than multiple t-tests?
Do I need to know the population standard deviation?

faq.a: It means the results are unlikely to have happened by pure chance alone. It does not necessarily mean the effect is large or important in the real world.
asks: Is statistical significance the same as practical significance?
Does a small p-value mean a big effect?

faq.q: What are the assumptions for running a test?
faq.a: Many tests assume the data is normally distributed and that the variances are equal across groups. Checking these assumptions is a crucial first step.
asks: What happens if my data isn't normal?

facts: Descriptive statistics summarize data using measures like mean, median, and mode.
Inferential statistics use sample data to make inferences about a larger population.
A low p-value (typically less than 0.05) suggests the results are statistically significant.
The choice of statistical test depends on the data type and the research design.

quiz.say: If you calculate the average score of five students, which measure are you using?
quiz.why: The mean is the mathematical average, which is what 'average' refers to in this context.

wrong.0: Standard deviation measures spread, not the central tendency of the scores.
wrong.2: The median is only correct if you list the scores in order and pick the middle one.
wrong.3: The mode is only correct if one score appears more often than any other score.

quiz.say: A researcher compares the test scores of students who used Method A versus Method B. Which test is most appropriate?
quiz.why: A t-test is specifically designed to compare the means of exactly two independent groups.

wrong.0: Chi-square tests are used for categorical data, not continuous scores like test scores.
wrong.2: Correlation measures the relationship between two variables, not the difference between two groups.
wrong.3: ANOVA is used when you compare the means of three or more groups at once.

quiz.say: If a p-value is 0.01, what does this suggest about the results?

options.show: The effect size is very small.
options.say: The effect size is very small.

options.show: You must use the median instead.
options.say: You must use the median instead.

options.show: The results are likely statistically significant.
options.say: The results are likely statistically significant.

quiz.why: Since 0.01 is less than the common threshold of 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis.

wrong.0: The p-value only tells you about chance, not the actual size or importance of the effect.
wrong.1: The p-value is a probability calculation and does not dictate which descriptive measure you must use.
wrong.3: A low p-value suggests the results are unlikely due to chance, not that they are meaningless.
